options: Replacing hard-coded inputs (users, search terms) with varied data, usually from a CSV file
Extracting server-generated values from responses
Running JMeter with command-line parameters only
Adding timers between requests
questions.explanation: Parameterization varies the inputs you choose. Extracting server values is correlation; -J options and timers are different topics.

questions.prompt: Which value is typically a correlation candidate?
options: A CSRF token in a hidden form field
The product name you choose to search for
The HTTP method
The server port
questions.explanation: CSRF tokens are generated by the server per session and must be extracted and re-sent. Search terms are test data, and method/port are static.

questions.prompt: A value that is the same in two recordings of the same journey may still need correlation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Some values only look static (e.g. long-lived but session-bound ids). Diffing recordings finds most dynamic values, but you still check what the server issues per session.

questions.prompt: A hidden field looks like `<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="9f8e7d"/>`. Which Regular Expression Extractor expression captures the value?
options: name="_csrf" value="(.+?)"
name="_csrf" value="(.+)"/>.*
_csrf
value=(\d+)
questions.explanation: A lazy group between the quotes captures just the token. The greedy version can run past the closing quote on longer pages, the bare name has no capture group, and \d+ misses hex letters.

questions.prompt: Which extractor is most robust for pulling a value out of an HTML form by element and attribute?
options: CSS Selector Extractor (e.g. input[name=_csrf] with attribute value)
Boundary Extractor with very long boundaries
Duration Assertion
XPath2 Extractor on a JSON response
questions.explanation: CSS selectors target the element directly and survive attribute order changes. Long boundaries are fragile, Duration Assertion does not extract, and XPath does not apply to JSON.

questions.prompt: Why does parameterizing search terms matter for performance results? Select all that apply.
options: Repeating one term lets caches serve everything, making results unrealistically fast
Varied data exercises realistic database query paths
It is only needed for functional testing
It avoids all users hitting the same row and creating artificial lock contention
questions.explanation: Same data skews caching and locking either way. Parameterization is therefore a performance concern, not just functional.

questions.prompt: Your extractor for `orderId` works, but the next request sends `orderId=NOT_FOUND` for about 3% of iterations. The JTL shows the create-order request returned HTTP 200 with an HTML 'Please try again' page in those cases. What is the best fix?
options: Add an assertion on create-order for the expected JSON (or the orderId) so those samples fail, and guard later steps with an If Controller on the variable
Change the default value to 0 so the next call succeeds
Increase the ramp-up
Remove the extractor's default value
questions.explanation: The real issue is an undetected failed response. Asserting turns it into a counted error, and an If Controller stops a broken chain. Fake defaults hide problems, and ramp-up or removing the default does not fix detection.

questions.prompt: An app allows one session per account. You need 300 concurrent users for 1 hour, each logging in once at the start. How do you configure CSV Data Set Config?
options: At least 300 unique accounts, Sharing mode All threads, Recycle False, Stop thread on EOF True, login inside a Once Only Controller
10 accounts with Recycle True
300 accounts with Sharing mode Current thread
One account shared by all threads
questions.explanation: Each thread needs its own account for the whole run, so rows must not be reused or recycled. Current thread mode makes every thread start from row 1, so all would use the same account.

coding.title: Extract a token and fill the next request
coding.prompt:
Write `next_body(html, template)`: extract the value of the hidden input named `_csrf` from `html` (attribute order may vary: `name` before or after `value`) and substitute it for `${csrf}` in `template`. If not found, substitute `NOT_FOUND`.

Example: html `<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="9f8e"/>` and template `user=bob&_csrf=${csrf}` gives `user=bob&_csrf=9f8e`.
coding.explanation: Finding the input tag first and then reading its value attribute works whatever the attribute order, the same reason CSS Selector Extractors are more robust than one long regex.
hints: Find each `<input ...>` tag with a regex.
Pick the tag containing `name="_csrf"`, then read `value="..."` from it.

tests.name: Value before name
tests.code: assert next_body('<input value="abc" name="_csrf"><input name="q" value="x">', 't=${csrf}') == 't=abc'

coding.title: How many accounts do you need?
coding.prompt:
Write `accounts_needed(concurrent_users, logins_per_user, one_session_per_account, reuse_after_logout)`:

- If `one_session_per_account` is False, 1 account is technically enough: return `1`.
- Otherwise each concurrent user needs its own account. If `reuse_after_logout` is True, accounts can be reused by later logins of the same thread, so return `concurrent_users`.
- If `reuse_after_logout` is False, every login needs a fresh account: return `concurrent_users * logins_per_user`.

Example: `accounts_needed(300, 4, True, False)` returns `1200`.
coding.explanation: Sizing test data is part of parameterization. Getting it wrong shows up as 'already logged in' errors that are script bugs, not system defects.
hints: With reuse, one account per concurrent user is enough.
Without reuse, multiply by logins per user.
